An August afternoon. You get off the train at Hibari Station.
Pulling a big suitcase, you have come to Japan alone for the first time. This is where you will live from now on.
Your heart is pounding. How do you feel right now?
I'm excited.
I'm a little worried.
I'm tired.
A new town. A new life. You want to go and explore right away.
Will I be able to speak Japanese well? But it's fine. One step at a time.
You want to rest early today. But there are things to do first.
There are a few big signs in the station. You want to go outside. Which one do you look at?
I look at the "deguchi" (exit) sign.
I look at the "iriguchi" (entrance) sign.
I ask a station attendant.
「入」 means going in, 「出」 means going out. 「入口」 is the way in. Let's look again.
The station attendant points to that green sign. It says 「出口」 (exit).
That green sign says 「出口」. Let's head that way.
Outside is a town with a beautiful sunset. A street lined with cherry trees stretches ahead.
Your phone buzzes. It's a message from the school.
"This is Hibari Japanese Academy. Welcome! Please come to school tomorrow morning at 9."
When do you have to go to school?
Tomorrow morning at 9.
Tonight at 9.
Next Monday.
Read the message again. It says 「明日の朝九時に」 (tomorrow morning at 9).
That's right. Tomorrow morning at 9. Put it in your phone so you don't forget.
You reply to the school. What do you write?
I understand. Thank you for your help.
I don't understand.
"OK" is fine with friends, but to the school write 「分かりました」.
But you did understand. Write 「分かりました」.
A reply comes right away. "Thank you. See you tomorrow."
You walk along Sakura Street. Bread smells good from the bakery. Someone is walking a dog.
You catch the eye of an old woman walking her dog. She is smiling. What do you do?
You say "konbanwa".
You bow.
You ignore her and walk past.
The old woman says "Good evening. What a lovely evening" and smiles.
The old woman bows too. Even without words, the feeling gets across.
The old woman looks a little sad. Tomorrow, try greeting people first.
Go back to your room at Hibari Heights.
You open the door of your small room. When you turn on the light, there's a white desk and a bed.
Do you try saying "tadaima" (I'm home)?
You say "tadaima".
You say nothing.
There's nobody here. But saying it quietly makes you feel a little calmer.
The room is quiet. But from tomorrow, this town will come alive.
Good night. Your life in Hibari-chō begins tomorrow.
